armF.summary: Meta temporarily pulled Muse’s human-call feature after admitting it had not properly explained that contractors might handle calls involving users’ sensitive information.
armF.prompt:
Below is a finished English news feature article (already translated from Japanese, no section headings). Write ONE short, natural sentence that captures the core of the story, in a way a listener can understand by hearing it just once.

Requirements:
- Exactly one sentence.
- Understandable on a single listen.
- Do not pack in multiple separate points; focus on the single most important point or twist of the story.
- Do not add any new fact, conclusion, or lesson that is not already stated in the article below.
- Keep who did what to whom, and what exactly it applied to, the same as in the Japanese source article and the Ledger below.

As a rough guide only (Trial-only guidance, not a strict rule): aim for one main clause with at most one subordinate clause, roughly 12-18 words.

Output only the sentence itself, nothing else (no quotation marks, no label like "In one line:", no Markdown heading markup).

[Article]
# Who Was on the Other End of the Phone? The Unexpected Roles in an AI Service

A human appeared in a situation where AI was supposed to make a phone call. This story begins with that slightly unusual casting. In some calls made through Muse, tests were carried out in which trained human contractors placed the calls and completed the conversations.

But this is not just a quiz about whether a human or AI made the call. In some cases, sensitive information from users may be needed to complete the conversation. Meta employees worried that when human contractors handled the calls, such information might be shared unintentionally with call center contractors.

The important thing here is not to make the story bigger than it is. This is not a story about a large-scale data leak. What was raised was a privacy concern: that information might be shared. In other words, the concern is less about the fact that a human helped and more about whether users were clearly told who might be involved in the conversation and might have access to their information. Even if a service looks smart on the surface, whether people can trust it is another question if they cannot see who is involved behind the scenes.

A Meta vice president admitted it was a mistake to start testing calls made by contractors without explaining this properly, and temporarily withdrew the human concierge feature. But the curtain came down only on the human concierge feature. Muse as a whole did not stop. What is worth watching this time is not only how smart AI is, but whether users are clearly told that people are involved behind the scenes. The “cast list” for a useful service seems to need an explanation that users can see, too.

[Japanese source article]
電話の向こうにいたのは誰？　AIサービスの意外な配役

AIが電話をかけるはずの場面に、人間が登場。今回の話は、そんな少し変わった配役から始まります。Muse経由の電話の一部では、訓練を受けた人間の契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを完了させるテストが行われていました。

でも、これは「電話をかけるのはAIか人間か」というクイズだけでは終わりません。やり取りを終えるために、ユーザーの機微な情報が必要になる場合があります。Metaの従業員は、人間の契約スタッフが電話を担当すると、そうした情報がコールセンターの契約スタッフに意図せず共有される可能性があると懸念しました。

ここで大事なのは、話を盛りすぎないこと。大規模な情報漏えいが起きたという話ではありません。示されたのは、情報が共有されるかもしれないというプライバシー上の懸念です。つまり、気になるのは人間が手伝ったこと自体より、誰が会話に関わり、ユーザーの情報に触れる可能性があるのかが、利用者に分かるよう説明されていたかどうか。サービスの表側がスマートでも、舞台裏の配役が見えなければ、安心して任せられるかは別問題です。

Metaの副社長は、適切な説明をしないまま契約スタッフが電話をかけるテストを始めたのはミスだったと認め、人間コンシェルジュ機能を当面取り下げました。ただし、幕が下りたのは人間コンシェルジュ機能だけ。Muse全体が止まったわけではありません。今回の見どころは、AIの賢さだけではなく、裏側で人が関わることまできちんと伝えられるか。便利なサービスの「配役表」には、利用者にも見える説明が必要そうです。

armR.final_summary: Meta temporarily rolled back Muse’s human-concierge feature after admitting it tested some contractor-handled calls without proper disclosure.
armR.final_text:
# Who Was on the Other End of the Phone? The Unexpected Roles in an AI Service

A human appeared in a situation where AI was supposed to make a phone call. This story begins with that slightly unusual casting. In some calls made through Muse, tests were carried out in which trained human contractors placed the calls and completed the conversations.

But this is not just a quiz about whether a human or AI made the call. In some cases, sensitive information from users may be needed to complete the conversation. Meta employees worried that when human contractors handled the calls, such information might be shared unintentionally with call center contractors.

The important thing here is not to make the story bigger than it is. This is not a story about a large-scale data leak. What was raised was a privacy concern: that information might be shared. In other words, the concern is less about the fact that a human helped and more about whether users were clearly told who might be involved in the conversation and might have access to their information. Even if a service looks smart on the surface, whether people can trust it is another question if they cannot see who is involved behind the scenes.

A Meta vice president admitted it was a mistake to start testing calls made by contractors without explaining this properly, and temporarily withdrew the human concierge feature. But the curtain came down only on the human concierge feature. Muse as a whole did not stop. What is worth watching this time is not only how smart AI is, but whether users are clearly told that people are involved behind the scenes. The “cast list” for a useful service seems to need an explanation that users can see, too.

## In one line
Meta temporarily rolled back Muse’s human-concierge feature after admitting it tested some contractor-handled calls without proper disclosure.
